items.abstract: <jats:p>Windows disk image forensic analysis remains constrained by the manual effort required to coordinate numerous specialized parsers and forensic utilities before substantive investigative reasoning can begin. Although large language models have recently been examined in digital forensics, existing studies have largely emphasized isolated model demonstrations, single-case evaluations, or question answering without access to case evidence. This paper presents ArshaLab, an open and modular platform for LLM-assisted Windows forensic investigation that integrates artifact collection through The Sleuth Kit, parsing of standard Windows forensic artifacts, indexing into Elasticsearch, and reasoning through interchangeable cloud-based and locally hosted LLMs, reachable through a web interface and a Model Context Protocol server. Its reasoning layer is governed by predefined evidence-retrieval anchors and protected by a structural anti-hallucination defense that combines a tool boundary, a field whitelist, and per-step source attribution to ground every model response in indexed evidence. We evaluate the platform across three Windows cases spanning a ransomware incident, a remote-access backdoor, and insider data exfiltration, and against a manual baseline obtained from twelve practitioners who worked the same cases without the platform. Cloud models achieve 89 to 97 percent key-entity recall with hallucination rates below 1.7 percent and shorten the phases the platform automates by more than an order of magnitude relative to this baseline. In a complementary chain reconstruction evaluation, all twelve evaluated model-case combinations produce no hallucinated fact under the evidence-grounding check. By releasing the implementation, dataset, and benchmarking harness, ArshaLab provides a reproducible foundation for evaluating forensic LLM systems across providers and deployment settings.</jats:p>
title: ArshaLab: A Modular Platform for LLM-Assisted Windows Forensic Investigation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Full self-attention in large language models scales as O(N 2), limiting long-context document analysis to 65,536 tokens and requiring costly GPU clusters. The Reduced Interaction Sampling (RIS) inference engine addresses this constraint as a model-agnostic architecture. Without modifying weights, RIS reduces self-attention complexity to O(N log N) using sparse stochastic geometry that fits within commodity memory limits. We validate RIS on Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct across two regimes. In controlled evaluations at 32,768 tokens (where native dense attention serves as the upper bound), RIS-Stochastic at 1% density and 70 ensemble seeds achieves 75.00% accuracy, outperforming the native dense baseline (71.88%), while RIS-Stochastic at 5% density and 10 seeds matches it (71.88%). This demonstrates that sparse attention acts as a regularizer: low density (1%) over multiple seeds filters out sequence-level noise, whereas higher density (5%) reintroduces distractor noise. Under the tightest budget, RIS-Structural reaches 68.75% accuracy at 1% density with just 10 seeds, recovering 75% of the contextual gap relative to the zero-context floor (59.38%). At 65,536 tokens, where dense attention triggers out-of-memory faults, RIS yields retrieval gains of up to 14.06 percentage points over the zero-context floor (51.56%). All evaluations run on commodity, unaccelerated CPU servers (16-128 GB of RAM), demonstrating that long-context LLM inference is feasible on standard academic hardware without GPU acceleration.</jats:p>
title: RIS-Kernel: A Model-agnostic Architecture for Long-context LLM Inference via Sparse Attention

items.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer devices raises practical concerns regarding inference latency and resource efficiency, which can vary depending on the operating system environment. However, it is still unknown which operating system is most optimal and efficient for executing local LLM workloads on hardware with limited resources. Therefore, this study aims to compare and evaluate the inference performance of LLMs across three operating system environments: native Windows, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2), and native Linux on a low-spec laptop equipped with a 12th Gen Intel Core i3 processor and 8 GB of RAM. The Ollama framework is used to run several lightweight LLM models, including Llama3.2:3B, Qwen2.5:3B, and Phi3.5:3.8B. An experimental benchmarking approach is conducted using three levels of prompt complexity (light, medium, and heavy), with 10 trials for each prompt scenario to ensure consistency of results. Evaluation metrics include inference latency, CPU utilization, and memory consumption during model execution. Results show that the operating system environment significantly impacts the inference performance of LLMs. For example, using the Llama3.2:3B model under heavy prompting, the average latency reaches 71.24 seconds on Windows, 75.96 seconds on WSL2, and 70.80 seconds on native Linux, while under light prompting the average latency is 11.76 seconds, 12.73 seconds, and 10.83 seconds, respectively. These findings indicate that native Linux generally provides more efficient LLM inference on resource-constrained hardware. This study contributes an empirical and repeatable comparison across operating system environments, providing practical insights for selecting deployment platforms for LLM applications.</jats:p>
title: LLM INFERENCE PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS ACROSS WINDOWS, WINDOWS SUBSYSTEM FOR LINUX 2 AND NATIVE LINUX

items.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into critical infrastructure, externally auditing their safety mechanism activation without internal access becomes essential. This paper investigates whether LLM safety refusals produce a detectable computational footprint at the operating system level across multi- modal side channels. We frame this as a Safety Mechanism Activation Detection problem, employing high-resolution eBPF kernel tracing and GPU telemetry to classify model outputs as Refusal or Compliance. Initial experiments on Meta Llama 3.1 8B yielded high predictive accuracy (AUC ≥ 0.93). However, a rigorous seven-phase analysis revealed this performance was driven entirely by a confounding variable: response length. To isolate genuine safety-mechanism- activation signatures, we applied Length-Controlled Matching, retaining only response pairs with identical token counts. When response length was strictly controlled, the predictive power of kernel and GPU features collapsed to ran- dom chance (AUC ≈ 0.50), despite concurrent white-box analysis proving that the model’s internal representations clearly distinguish safety contexts (AUC 0.84-0.89). We therefore propose the Kernel Blindness hypothesis: under strictly bounded compute environments (single-GPU, 4-bit quantized, non-batched dense transformer inference), the semantic intent of neural operations is indistinguish- able at the kernel level. This phenomenon is rigorously confirmed across three major 7-8B model architectures (Llama 3.1, Gemma, and Mistral), demonstrat- ing that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) safety alignment produces no externally detectable computational signatures under these specific constraints. This overarching negative result highlights a fundamental limita- tion in black-box monitoring for edge deployments and emphasizes the need for grey-box auditing approaches.
title: The Kernel Blindness Hypothesis: Investigating OS-Level Detectability of LLM Safety Mechanisms

items.abstract: <jats:p>The use of unsupported Windows systems can pose a significant security risk for users and organizations alike. This paper examines why individual users and organizations continue to use unsupported versions of Windows. Whether it is due to inconvenience, lack of resources, bad prior experiences, or compatibility issues with operational technology. It offers warnings against using unsupported Windows systems because they no longer receive support, have well-known vulnerabilities, and can compromise networks. Examples of major data breaches are given that were caused or exacerbated by unpatched/outdated systems. The paper explores and even demonstrates an infamous Windows exploit called EternalBlue using Metasploit and an unpatched Windows 7 virtual machine, as well as some of the malware/ransomware that came about because of it. Guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publications 800-40, 800-53, and 800-94 is explored, such as patch management, flaw remediation, backup/recovery, and intrusion detection methods. It also explores strategies for mitigating risk associated with unsupported systems, such as segmentation, role-based access control, and attribute-based access control.</jats:p>
title: Security Risks of Unsupported Windows Systems

items.abstract: Large-language-model agent systems increasingly combine multiple agents, tools, persistent state, and external effects, while logical identity and authority may remain entangled with transient runtime or session objects. We evaluate World 8, an experimental shared governance kernel that separates a logical Actor from provider/session/runtime identity and combines effect-time authorization, fencing, tamper-evident evidence, and recovery-before-effect constraints. A falsification-oriented program first strengthens a session-scoped baseline with revocation checks, compare-and-swap versioning, durable idempotency, approval scope, and audit. In 98,000 reference-model trials, the hardened baseline matches World 8 on those generic mechanisms, narrowing the differentiated tested composition. The same kernel and eight-invariant suite are then applied to Company and Trading Society adapters for 1,000 trials each, producing identical all-pass conformance vectors without market-performance evaluation or live effects. Canonical-source/runtime probes confirm selected authorization, fencing, immutability, actor/work binding, and recovery behavior. A scoped mutation stage kills 5/5 controlled mutations, and compound-fault tests preserve the frozen valid paths without false denials. Finally, 2,000 cases execute on real AutoGen Core 0.7.5. Generic hardening closes revocation, CAS, and idempotency faults; a transparent World-8-style governance wrapper additionally closes the frozen stolen-approval, stale-fence, audit-tamper, and effect-before-recovery cases. The evidence supports a bounded, composable effect-governance architecture, not standalone novelty for agent identity/governance primitives, general framework superiority, or production readiness.
title: A Governed Shared-Kernel Architecture for Persistent, Auditable Multi-Agent Societies Beyond the LLM Session

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper investigates adaptive Markov controllers with internal memory that is not observable at the plant level. The main contribution is a separation-and-interface framework connecting exact Touchette--Lloyd one-step entropy accounting with metric surrogate-validity certification. The entropy layer establishes an exact plant--joint gap identity, showing that plant-only analysis omits the one-step change in conditional memory uncertainty. This identity measures hidden-memory burden, but it does not by itself provide metric control. The metric layer is therefore supplied by the model class through a memory-space geometry, posterior dispersion, and effective-kernel sensitivity. Standard total-variation contraction then propagates the resulting kernel mismatch into a finite-horizon validity window. Within this certified window, a representative-memory plant surrogate supports plant-level one-step information analysis on a surrogate law whose finite-horizon distributional error is explicitly bounded in total variation. The main certificate uses a rolling representative recomputed from the current posterior, while a complementary frozen-memory comparison is analyzed separately on the augmented state space. The framework gives a diagnostic evaluation of plant-level surrogate reliability and identifies the factors that must be controlled to obtain bounded hidden-memory effects over operational horizons.</jats:p>
title: A Touchette–Lloyd Framework for Adaptive Markov Control: Validity Windows for Surrogate Kernel Reduction

items.abstract: <jats:p>Memory objects in the kernel often remain accessible long after their safe lifetime, leading to use-after-free exploits. We present a lifetime-aware isolation model that assigns temporal protection windows to kernel objects. PKS permissions are revoked when objects exit valid lifetime states. Applied to six kernel allocators (SLUB, SLOB, SLAB), the technique eliminates 67% of UAF exploitability cases** and shortens exposure windows by 72%. Benchmarking shows ≤4% overhead across memory-intensive workloads. This temporal model adds a new dimension to kernel compartmentalization by aligning memory protection with object lifecycles.</jats:p>
title: Lifetime-Aware Kernel Object Isolation Using Temporal Protection Windows

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>This paper delves into the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) as they pertain to national security, with a particular emphasis on their integration into military applications. Through an in-depth analysis of the United States' progress in assimilating AI technologies into the battle space, the paper seeks to reinvigorate enthusiasm about the potential of AI in safeguarding national interests. Key aspects of this paper include the necessity of protecting AI systems from adversaries, as well as the inherent challenges and risks that come with integrating them into military operations. The paper concludes by underscoring the strategic significance of AI in the realm of national security and outlines a set of strategic imperatives for military leaders and policymakers to ensure success in this critical domain.</p></jats:p>
title: Optimizing National Security Strategies through LLM-Driven Artificial Intelligence Integration

items.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence and machine learning continue to advance, we must understand their strategic importance in national security. This paper focuses on unique AI applications in the military, emphasizes strategic imperatives for success, and aims to rekindle excitement about AI's role in national security. We will examine the United States progress in integrating AI into the battle space, discuss the importance of securing these technologies from adversaries, and explore the challenges and risks associated with their integration. Finally, we will highlight the strategic significance of AI to national security and a set of strategic imperatives for military leaders and policymakers.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Dalam era digital yang semakin maju, perangkat lunak menjadi kunci bagi produktivitas, kreativitas, dan konektivitas manusia. Salah satu sistem operasi yang dominan adalah Windows, Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menyelidiki risiko keamanan dan penggunaan perangkat lunak tidak resmi, khususnya dalam konteks Windows, yang merupakan sistem operasi yang paling banyak digunakan di dunia. Berdasarkan latar belakang tersebut, penulis menjalankan penelitian dengan metode wawancara, survei, dan studi pustaka. Wawancara dilakukan dengan ahli komputer untuk memahami masalah keamanan dan batasan penggunaan Windows tidak resmi. Ditemukan bahwa penggunaan Windows tidak resmi dapat mengakibatkan keterbatasan keamanan, gangguan sistem, dan fungsionalitas yang terbatas. Selanjutnya, studi pustaka mengungkapkan berbagai kerentanan keamanan dalam Windows tidak resmi serta dampaknya terhadap pengguna dan organisasi. Solusi yang disarankan adalah beralih ke Windows resmi atau distribusi Linux, dengan meningkatkan kesadaran masyarakat tentang risiko penggunaan perangkat lunak bajakan. Survei dilakukan untuk memahami persepsi dan pengalaman pengguna terhadap Windows tidak resmi. Mayoritas responden mengaku tidak yakin dengan keamanan sistem operasi Windows tidak resmi yang mereka gunakan dan mengalami gangguan sistem atau masalah fungsionalitas. Alasan penggunaan Windows tidak resmi antara lain kurangnya pemahaman tentang perbedaan versi resmi dan tidak resmi serta ketersediaan dan harga yang lebih murah. Dengan demikian, penelitian ini menyimpulkan bahwa edukasi tentang risiko penggunaan perangkat lunak bajakan penting untuk meningkatkan kesadaran masyarakat dan mendorong penggunaan solusi yang aman dan legal</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adversarial attacks pose an important threat to the security and trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs). These models are vulnerable to carefully engineered input designed to exploit their weaknesses, degrade system performance, and extract private information. Practical countermeasures need a strong offensive strategy that includes adversarial scenarios simulation to test how models hold up in various conditions. Adversarial data poisoning and evasion techniques are particularly useful as they can reveal strengths during training and inference processes, respectively. Through systematic identification and mitigation of every vulnerability, organizations can strengthen the model's robustness to real-world attacks. This technical framework also emphasizes the need to embed adversarial simulations into the security cycle of LLMs to prevent risks associated with malicious actors. Via iterative analysis, an organization can increase the robustness of a model and build a resilient infrastructure for secure implementation of LLMs in sensitive/high-level environments.</jats:p>
title: LLM Security and Guardrail Defense Techniques in Web Applications

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of large language models (LLMs) into mobile applications introduces new vectors for security and privacy vulnerabilities. This study proposes an automated framework for systematically testing LLM-enabled mobile apps, focusing on identifying potential threats such as prompt injection, data leakage, unauthorized access, and adversarial manipulation. The approach combines dynamic analysis, static code inspection, and machine learning-based anomaly detection to evaluate app behaviors in real-time. Our method ensures scalability and efficiency across diverse mobile platforms and LLM configurations. Results demonstrate significant improvements in detection rates and response times compared to conventional manual testing. This work aims to bridge the gap between AI innovation and secure mobile deployment, promoting trust in AI-integrated ecosystems.</jats:p>

<jats:p>The prevailing literature suggests that large language model (LLM) systems remain vulnerable to prompt injection and other adversarial inputs, while existing LLM-based defenses do not provide deterministic assurance against such attacks. This paper therefore treats the LLM as insecure.It follows that a mechanism intended to secure an LLM must itself be independent of LLM technology. For sufficiently bounded domains, this paper proposes a deterministic front end that permits only validated, structured representations of user requests to cross a trust boundary protecting the LLM and security-critical information. The front end neither requires nor assumes an LLM; what consumes its output is irrelevant to its operation. 
<div>
 The paper further proposes that this front end can take the form of a deterministic natural-language interface (NLI), preserving the flexibility of an LLM-style prompt interface. Rather than attempting to anticipate all possible expressions, the NLI can be developed from a corpus of actual domain interactions using techniques derived from pre-LLM speech recognition and natural-language processing. The resulting classifier deterministically maps recognized input to permitted structured representations and rejects ambiguous, incomplete, or out-of-domain input.
</div>
<div>
 If sufficiently comprehensive, such an NLI may, at least for ordinary legitimate queries, be functionally indistinguishable to the user from a domainrestricted probabilistic LLM interface, while ensuring that unvalidated user input never crosses the trust boundary
</div></jats:p>
title: Securing Bounded-Domain LLM Systems Using Deterministic Natural-Language Security Gateways

<jats:p><p>The rapid enterprise deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic AI systems has outpaced the security practices required to operate them safely. Traditional penetration testing methodologies — built on deterministic system assumptions — fail to address the probabilistic, natural-language attack surface introduced by AI deployments. This paper presents a structured, five-phase practitioner framework for LLM and agentic AI security testing, grounded in documented real-world attack patterns and aligned to OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), OWASP Agentic Top 10 (2026), and MITRE ATLAS v5.1.0. The framework addresses four critical attack classes — indirect prompt injection via RAG corpus poisoning, agentic goal hijacking through multi-turn social engineering, system prompt leakage, and MCP tool poisoning — providing exploitation methodology, detection engineering guidance, and MITRE ATLAS technique mappings for each. Defensive countermeasures are presented across prevention, detection, and response layers, including sample detection logic for integration into SIEM and CI/CD pipelines. The paper establishes that organizations deploying AI systems without AI-specific security testing face material risks of data exfiltration, unauthorized autonomous action, and regulatory violation — and that a structured methodology mapped to existing frameworks is sufficient to close the execution gap.</p>
<p></p></jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Trace-level characterization is a promising approach for understanding how adversarial influence propagates through resource-operating LLM agents, but current agent-security benchmarks and vulnerability disclosures collapse this propagation into binary outcomes or endpoint categories that obscure where attacks actually stopped. Recent benchmark-audit work has questioned the evidentiary support behind agent-security scores, yet the trace-level propagation structure inside those scores remains uncharacterized. This paper first proposes the Agentic Influence Propagation Framework (AIPF), a trace-level propagation framework with an applicability criterion based on three adversarial objective categories, an exposure marker X, three propagation levels (L1 operational commitment, L2 action materialization, L3 resource realization), and orthogonal episode annotations, and applies it to 180 AgentDojo traces through a three-annotator study spanning senior, junior, and non-specialist expertise. The analysis shows that 4 of 98 benchmark-defended traces reach L3 and 26 of 81 benchmark-successful traces show only shallow propagation, distinctions that the binary outcome collapses. Three case-study groups-a controlled CTF trace, a redacted cloud-agent vulnerability, and four public CVEs-further illustrate the vocabulary's reach beyond benchmark settings. This study provides a structured language for describing where agentic attacks stop and why, and extracts useful distinctions that can inform benchmark design, defence engineering, and agent-specific vulnerability reporting.</jats:p>
title: Beyond Binary Success: Propagation Profiles for LLM Agent Security Traces

items.abstract: <jats:p>Quick Response (QR) codes are now widely used as a digital communication tool. However, their extensive adoption has made them an attractive target for cyberattacks, particularly through the injection of malicious URLs that redirect users to phishing sites or initiate malware installations. Conventional security approaches such as blacklists and antivirus software are no longer efficient against such evolving threats. This vision paper proposes an AI-based framework using fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify malicious URLs embedded within QR codes. To ensure transparency, a novel ensemble Explainable AI (XAI) is applied to aggregate insights from various XAI methods to explain the features influencing model predictions, facilitating more robust interpretations. To enhance clarity and usability, the proposed framework incorporates personalized explanations tailored to cybersecurity analysts, system developers, and non-expert end users, informed by a role-specific user study. Furthermore, as XAI methods may expose sensitive model behavior, cyberattackers craft adversarial inputs to mislead the model or manipulate explanations. This necessitates the integration of adversarial training to ensure model robustness and explanation integrity, evaluated through perturbation consistency checks. The paper outlines key challenges in explanation fidelity and personalization and presents a development roadmap to advance secure, transparent, and human-centric explainable QR code analysis.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Linux kernel specialization can improve system efficiency, but configuration changes may also alter functionality, compatibility, and security. Performance gains are difficult to interpret unless the configuration that was realized and executed is established. Existing configuration-tailoring, performance-search, and LLM-assisted methods address parts of this problem separately. They do not connect workload-derived evidence, model proposals, deterministic Kconfig realization, booted-state identity, empirical performance, and deployment-policy compliance in one auditable process. Intelligent Kernel Configuration (IKC) addresses this gap through an evidence-bounded workflow. Workload traces guide candidate selection, and local Kconfig knowledge constrains LLM-assisted editing. Deterministic configuration tools establish realizable states, while boot-time configurations define experimental identity. Repeated measurements provide performance evidence, and an explicit policy gate determines deployment eligibility. Across representative web-serving, database, storage, media-processing, and scheduler workloads, IKC produced workload-dependent improvements over conventional configurations. Several workload classes retained supported advantages over machine-tailored alternatives. Evidence for the contribution of trace conditioning was more concentrated, and explicit hardening constraints preserved much of the measured performance. Complementary network-path and performance-oriented comparisons were consistent with this interpretation. These findings position model assistance within a traceable realization and validation framework, linking generated recommendations to explicit system evidence and operational outcomes. The resulting workflow establishes a reproducible foundation for workload-aware kernel specialization under well-defined operational constraints.</jats:p>
title: IKC: Auditing LLM-Assisted Linux Kernel Configuration with Workload Evidence

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate and timely fault detection in strongly coupled industrial processes is crucial for maintaining product quality, reducing unplanned downtime, and improving energy and resource efficiency. However, practical monitoring remains challenging because process data are typically high-dimensional, nonlinear, nonstationary, and are frequently affected by noise, while faults may exhibit diverse temporal patterns (e.g., fast transients and slow drifts) under multimode operating conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes an integrated monitoring framework that combines singular spectrum analysis (SSA), multi-scale sliding window (MSSW) feature extraction, and a multi-kernel principal component analysis (MKPCA) model. SSA is employed as a robust denoising module to suppress measurement disturbances while preserving the dominant dynamics. MSSW then constructs parallel temporal views using multiple window lengths, enabling simultaneous characterization of short-term fluctuations and long-term evolution. Based on these representations, an MKPCA model with kernel fusion is developed: candidate kernels are screened using an HSIC-based dependence score and further filtered under a diversity constraint to reduce redundancy. For online monitoring, the squared prediction error and the dissimilarity statistic are standardized and fused with robust normalization, and control limits are calibrated from normal data using quantile-based thresholds to stabilize false alarms. Experiments on a simulated nonlinear coupled process, the benchmark simulation model number 1 wastewater treatment benchmark, and a real-world papermaking dataset demonstrate robust detection performance under multimode and dynamically evolving conditions, offering a practical and flexible monitoring paradigm for complex industrial processes.</jats:p>
title: Fault Detection of Nonlinear Industrial Processes Based on Multi-Scale Sliding Windows and Multi-Kernel Principal Component Analysis

items.abstract: <jats:p>With the development of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology, multimachine collaborative operations have become the core model for increasing mission effectiveness. However, large-scale UAV clusters face challenges such as dynamic security threats, heterogeneous data fusion difficulties, and resource-constrained decision-making delays. Traditional single-machine intelligent architectures have limitations when addressing new threats, such as insufficient real-time response capabilities. To address these issues, this paper presnts an LLM-layered collaborative security architecture (LLM-LCSA) for multimachine collaborative security. This architecture optimizes the spatiotemporal fusion efficiency of multisource asynchronous data through cloud–edge–end collaborative deployment, combining an end lightweight LLM, an edge medium LLM, and a cloud-based foundation LLM. Additionally, a Mixture of Experts (MoEs) intelligent algorithm that dynamically activates the most relevant expert models by leveraging a threat–expert association matrix is introduced, thereby increasing the accuracy of complex threat identification and dynamic adaptability. Moreover, a resource-aware multi-objective optimization model is constructed to generate optimal decisions under resource constraints. Simulation results indicate that compared with traditional methods, LLM-LCSA achieves an average 7.92% improvement in the threat detection accuracy, reduces the system’s total response time by 44.52%, and enables resource scheduling during off-peak periods. This architecture provides an efficient, intelligent, and scalable solution for secure collaboration among UAV swarms. Future research should further explore its application potential in 6G network integration and large-scale swarm environments.</jats:p>
title: LLM-LCSA: LLM for Collaborative Control and Decision Optimization in UAV Cluster Security

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly combine probabilistic language interpretation with retrieval, persistent memory, external tools, and delegated enterprise credentials. This creates a system-security problem in which untrusted semantic content can cross trust boundaries and acquire operational authority. Existing work provides prompt-injection attacks, agent benchmarks, risk taxonomies, and governance guidance, but less directly addresses how those threats should be translated into verifiable controls for a deployed application. This paper presents a trust-boundary security assurance framework for LLM-integrated and agentic systems. The framework models the application as a mediated-authority system, identifies six architectural threat surfaces and seven recurring trust boundaries, and represents attack paths through source, mechanism, boundary, privilege, asset, and outcome. It then operationalizes the model through a six-stage assurance process covering system decomposition, authority mapping, adversarial scenario construction, boundary-control verification, containment and detection analysis, and evidence-based reporting. A dedicated Model Context Protocol (MCP) profile distinguishes protocol security, semantic trust, and enterprise authorization. The framework further connects defensive controls to observable evidence and proposes a decomposed measurement profile covering attack success, boundary interception, benign-task preservation, blast-radius characteristics, detection latency, and undetected events. A worked enterprise RAG--MCP scenario illustrates how the framework traces an indirect injection from retrieved content through delegated authority to an authorization decision and auditable evidence. The contribution is methodological rather than an empirical claim of defense superiority: it provides a traceable structure for converting evolving LLM and agent threats into testable security claims and application-level assurance evidence.
title: Beyond Prompt Injection: Trust-Boundary Security Assurance for LLM-Integrated and Agentic Applications

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into enterprise and institutional workflows that process sensitive and confidential information including K-12 systems. While security frameworks and guidance documents describe prominent LLM risks and recommended mitigations, K-12 schools still struggle to prioritize controls under real-world constraints. Existing approaches often provide qualitative checklists without a defensible method for selecting mitigations that most effectively reduce high-impact risk.This exploratory research presents an ontology-driven, graph-theoretic framework for prioritizing K-12 LLM security mitigations with a specific focus on confidentiality impact. Using a source LLM security ontology, we construct a multi-layered directed graph linking LLM functions, products, security risks, adversarial techniques, and mitigations. High-confidentiality functions are used as seeds in a function-seeded Personalized PageRank (PPR) analysis to identify attack techniques most structurally exposed to sensitive workflows. To evaluate mitigation effectiveness, we apply eight complementary graph analyses spanning combinatorial optimization, centrality, flow-based separation, stochastic modeling, and community detection.Across analyses, results converge on a small subset of mitigations, most notably AI telemetry logging and generative AI guardrails, as structurally dominant defenses. These controls collectively intercept a disproportionate share of PPR-weighted technique exposure, form low-cost barriers in cut-based analyses, and exhibit high probabilistic interception. Convergence across distinct objectives suggests stable structural bottlenecks rather than artifacts of graph size or algorithm choice. By integrating semantic richness from security ontologies with established attack-graph analytics, the exploratory research provides an approach for selecting high-impact mitigations in confidentiality-sensitive K-12 LLM deployments.
title: Ontology-Driven Graph Framework for Prioritizing K-12 LLM Security Mitigations

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Model (LLM)-driven coding agents have evolved from inline code completion utilities into autonomous systems capable of executing shell commands, modifying file hierarchies, retrieving remote documentation, and invoking external APIs. This expanded operational autonomy introduces security vulnerabilities that conventional software permission architectures fail to mediate. In this paper, we examine the attack surface created when autonomous programming agents are granted broad access to system-level tools. We propose Gated Autonomy, an architectural framework that enforces the principle of least privilege across the entire tool-execution lifecycle. The framework couples three defensive layers: a declarative policy gate enforcing static capability boundaries and parameter whitelisting, a runtime context evaluator tracking data provenance and privilege accumulation, and a postexecution audit engine providing counterfactual verification against temporal causal manipulation. We evaluate Gated Autonomy against a comprehensive taxonomy of fifteen documented attack vectors drawn from commercial coding assistants and open-source agent runtimes. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that the framework completely mitigates direct tool hijacking and cross-tool privilege escalation while reducing developer verification interruptions by over 80% through selective escalation.</jats:p>
title: Gated Autonomy: A Layered Security Framework for Tool Access Governance in LLM-Driven Coding Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Integrating large language models (LLMs) into intelligent connected vehicles (ICVs) introduces cyber–physical security risks: semantically plausible instructions may still trigger unsafe, safety-critical actions. Existing defenses are limited because they either lack physical grounding or rely on centralized filtering that cannot meet real-time constraints. We propose PSEVGuard, a cloud–edge security framework based on physical-semantic entanglement validation (PSEV). PSEV validates cross-modal consistency between semantic intent and physical context at the edge within strict latency budgets, while the cloud performs asynchronous adversarial analysis and policy refinement without blocking execution. In experiments under realistic threat models, PSEVGuard achieves a 98.7% attack interception rate with 0.8% false rejection, and maintains 99.2% task completion for benign inputs. The results indicate that enforcing physical–semantic consistency effectively constrains the attack surface of LLM-enabled cyber–physical systems.</jats:p>
title: PSEVGuard: Cloud–Edge Cyber–Physical LLM Security for Intelligent Connected Vehicles

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) for alert triage and threat‑intelligence synthesis. We study Adversarial Hallucination Engineering (AHE): attacks that bias LLM reasoning by introducing small clusters of poisoned context into retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, producing targeted fabrications aligned with attacker goals. Using a safe, fully synthetic simulator of a RAG+LLM SOC, we formalize the AHE threat model, introduce Hallucination Propagation Chains (HPCs)—mutually reinforcing poisoned documents designed to create artificial consensus at retrieval time—and evaluate a lightweight defense, Chain‑of‑Thought Attestation (CoTA), based on per‑token uncertainty, provenance attribution, and source reputation. Across three model scales, hallucination‑induction rate (HIR) rises superlinearly with HPC size (e.g., for a Large‑70B proxy, 12.45%→61.84% as HPC size in top‑k grows 0→5); actionable misconfiguration rate (AMR) grows from 3.23% (no attack) to 38.18% (HPC‑5). CoTA reduces attack‑success rate (ASR) by ~55% for HPCs≥3 at ~7% false‑positive flags and ~8% latency overhead. We release synthetic artifacts to support reproducible, defensive research.</jats:p>
title: Adversarial Hallucination Engineering: Targeted Misdirection Attacks Against LLM Powered Security Operations Centers

items.abstract: <jats:p>We propose a distillation framework that transfers secure coding expertise into a compact model trained using expert demonstrations, static-analysis labels, and secure patterns. The distilled model (7B parameters) achieves 83% security compliance, nearly matching GPT-4's 89% performance while requiring significantly less compute. Evaluated across CWE-20, CWE-78, CWE-89, the distilled model reduces injection vulnerabilities by 62% relative to baseline models. This work demonstrates that targeted distillation can teach smaller models to respect security best practices.</jats:p>
title: Security Knowledge Distillation for Enhancing LLM Safety in Code Generation Authors

items.abstract: <jats:p>In the field of Information Retrieval (IR), user-submitted keyword queries often fail to accurately represent users’ true search intent. With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly in natural language processing (NLP), query expansion (QE) based on large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a key strategy for improving retrieval effectiveness. However, such methods often introduce query topic drift, which negatively impacts retrieval accuracy and efficiency. To address this issue, this study proposes an LLM-based QE framework that incorporates a Gaussian kernel-enhanced semantic space for dense retrieval. Specifically, the model first employs LLMs to expand the semantic dimensions of the initial query, generating multiple query representations. Then, by introducing a Gaussian kernel semantic space, it captures deep semantic relationships among these query vectors, refining their semantic distribution to better represent the original query’s intent. Finally, the ColBERTv2 model is utilized to retrieve documents based on the enhanced query representations, enabling precise relevance assessment and improving retrieval performance. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, extensive empirical evaluations were conducted on the MS MARCO passage ranking dataset. The model was systematically assessed using key metrics, including MAP, NDCG@10, MRR@10, and Recall@1000. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches across multiple metrics, significantly improving retrieval precision while effectively mitigating query drift, offering a novel approach for building efficient QE mechanisms.</jats:p>
title: LLM-Based Query Expansion with Gaussian Kernel Semantic Enhancement for Dense Retrieval

items.abstract: <jats:p>Automating interactions with security-sensitive web services remains difficult due to dynamic frontends, session-bound tokens, and undocumented parameter-generation logic. Traditionally, developers must manually analyze captured traffic, hypothesize parameter-generation routines, and iteratively test internally defined functions until the interaction succeeds. We propose ASG-LLM, an execution grounded pipeline that generates scraping modules from a single successful browser session trace. ASG-LLM captures full HTTP(S) traffic, removes irrelevant requests through multi-stage filtering, and constructs a dependency-aware representation of the core interaction flow. When security-critical parameters cannot be reconstructed from the trace alone, the FUNC Retriever identifies a small set of reusable internal function descriptions using HyDE-guided selective retrieval, enabling the LLM to select compatible parameter-generation routines based on behavioral similarity rather than keyword matching, without exposing proprietary implementation code. Generated modules are executed in a controlled environment and iteratively repaired using structured failure feedback. ASG-LLM was evaluated on representative banking and public-sector portals. In our case studies, ASG-LLM reduces developer effort by cutting traffic analysis and basic code implementation from hours to minutes and reducing security-handling effort from a full-day task to a couple of hours. At the model level, HyDE-based selective retrieval improves internal function recommendation accuracy from 30% to 70% Top-1 and from 60% to 90% Top-3 compared with a full-context baseline. These results suggest that combining trace grounding, selective retrieval, and execution-time validation is a promising direction for robust web automation in security-constrained environments.</jats:p>
title: ASG-LLM: An LLM-Based Pipeline for Automated Scraping Code Generation in Security-Sensitive Environments

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in cloud-native environments has introduced unprecedented security challenges that traditional cybersecurity frameworks fail to adequately address. This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of LLM security threats in cloud infrastructures, examining 65 recent studies and real-world incidents from 2023-2025. We propose a novel taxonomy that categorizes threats into four primary dimensions: Infrastructure Security (credential theft, resource abuse), Application Security (prompt injection, data exfiltration), Model Security (model poisoning, adversarial attacks), and Supply Chain Security (dependency vulnerabilities, malicious packages). Our analysis reveals that LLMjacking attacks have increased 10x in 2024, with single incidents costing victims up to $100,000 per day. We identify critical research gaps, including the lack of standardized security frameworks for LLM-integrated applications and insufficient real-time threat detection capabilities. This survey synthesizes current defensive strategies, evaluates their effectiveness, and proposes future research directions toward achieving secure and trustworthy LLM deployments in cloud environments. Our findings provide actionable insights for security architects, cloud engineers, and researchers working to establish robust security postures for AI-powered cloud applications.</jats:p>
title: LLM Security in Cloud-Native Architectures: A Comprehensive Survey of Attacks, Defenses, and Operational Challenges

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper addresses the problem of ensuring security for C/C++ software systems, where static code analysis serves as a key tool for vulnerability detection but remains costly to maintain due to the complexity of developing rules and taint specifications. Existing approaches are analyzed: industrial static analyzers (Svace, Irbis), IFDS analysis, ML/NN-based solutions, and hybrid schemes involving large language models (LLMs) used for warning filtering, code generation, and automatic rule synthesis (QLPro, KNighter, CodePatchLLM). It is shown that direct use of LLMs as standalone vulnerability detectors yields high recall but is accompanied by a significant number of false positives and hallucinations. As an alternative, a multi-agent module for the SAST tool CodeQL, tailored for C/C++, is proposed. It leverages LLMs for the generation, validation, and evolution of rules in the QL query language within a closed loop of "generation, verification, refinement, filtering, ranking". The system architecture is described, featuring generator, validator, refiner, filter, and ranker agents, whose orchestration is implemented using LangGraph and PostgreSQL. Rule validation is performed against CodeQL databases Juliet, SARD, and real-world projects, with calculation of metrics including Precision, Recall, F1, FPR, and Specificity, and consideration of CVSS scores. This enables the selection of rules of acceptable quality and reduces the burden on developers through automated evolution of the rule base.</jats:p>
title: LLM-based multi-agent system for generation and evolution of CodeQL static analysis rules for C/C++

                  <ns4:p>
                    <ns4:bold>Conclusions:</ns4:bold>
                    In this paper, we have provided recommendations to Microsoft to improve their Windows Security tool through the use of Artificial intelligence (AI).

items.abstract: <jats:p>Attack success rates alone do not establish the security of large language model (LLM) systems because results depend on the attacker, deployment conditions, and measured consequence. This survey complements existing attack and defense taxonomies by examining what individual experiments actually support. We pair a threat model describing attacker capabilities and objectives with a defense model specifying observable information, security functions, and enforceable responses. An attack-defense assurance matrix determines whether an evaluation addresses the conditions relevant to a stated security claim. A bounded claim grammar also records the attacker, system version, consequence, cost, evaluation oracle, and other conditions that limit the result. An evidence ladder organizes empirical requirements for a fixed security claim and threat model without ranking papers or defenses. We apply the framework across model behavior, retrieval and memory, agents and tools, supply chains, privacy, availability, and serving infrastructure. The resulting synthesis helps researchers and practitioners distinguish demonstrated protection from untested conditions, compare results under matched assumptions, and design evaluations that measure the security consequences relevant to deployment.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating Security Claims in LLM Systems: A Survey of Adversarial Attacks and Defenses

items.abstract: <jats:p>Security prompts often contain multiple goals-e.g., analyzing a code snippet, describing its behavior, identifying vulnerabilities, and suggesting patches. Such multi-intent prompts lead to diluted reasoning in LLMs. We propose a decomposition pipeline that separates prompts into atomic intent units guided by a lightweight classifier trained on 18,000 annotated prompts across secure coding, configuration auditing, and API misuse detection tasks. Experiments with GPT-4, Gemini, and Llama-3 show that decomposition improves vulnerability detection F1-score from 0.61 to 0.83, while reducing irrelevant reasoning by 44%. Developers reported 36% improved interpretability in explanations. The results demonstrate that splitting complex prompts substantially enhances LLM reliability in security settings.</jats:p>
title: Multi-Intent Prompt Decomposition for Improving LLM Decision Quality in Security Auditing
